https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: Germanyâs far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is poised for a historic breakthrough in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, opening the prospect of the party seeking to govern despite falling short of an outright majority.With most interim results counted, the AfD was projected to secure a record 44% of the vote and far ahead of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which stood at 17%.Ulrich Siegmund, the AfDâs prominent leader in Saxony-Anhalt, described the result as âsensationalâ and said the party wanted to begin governing as soon as possible.According to the BBC report, a victory would mark an unprecedented development in post-war Germany, where no far-right party has previously taken control of a state government. State-level power would give the AfD influence over areas including policing, education and culture.Saxony-Anhalt, home to about 2.1 million people, has been a particular focus of concern because the stateâs AfD branch is classified as âright-wing extremistâ by Germanyâs domestic intelligence service. Siegmund, 35, rejects the designation.Siegmund and the partyâs national co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, celebrated as exit polls showed the AfD was on course to more than double its 2021 vote share.The AfDâs strong performance was quickly described by political opponents and commentators as a major turning point, highlighting the growing influence of the far-right party in German politics. Public broadcaster Das Erste even replaced its long-running crime drama Tatort with special coverage examining the significance of the result.âThis isnât just about Saxony-Anhalt,â Siegmund told supporters. âItâs a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal.âCommentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant.âThis result is not just about Saxony-Anhalt,â Siegmund told supporters, calling it âa signal for the whole of Germany â a confident signal.âThe result also drew attention abroad. US President Donald Trump shared a screenshot of the German election projection on his Truth Social platform, which Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev later reposted, describing the outcome as a âhistoric win for the pragmatic AfDâ.Dmitriev had previously praised the Russia-friendly party as one offering âhope and reasonâ and greater cooperation for Germany. US Vice-President JD Vance also backed the AfD ahead of Germanyâs federal election last year, a move that drew criticism in Germany over alleged foreign political interference.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, however, offered a sharply contrasting reaction. The centre-right leader said that in Poland, âonly idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD.âDespite its strong performance, the AfD lacks the seats needed to govern alone, leaving Ulrich Siegmund facing a difficult path to power. He has so far ruled out leading a minority government, even as the partyâs national leadership considers that option possible.Siegmund said the AfD would instead be willing to seek support from individual lawmakers or another party. âIf necessary thereâll just be new elections, then weâd just get 50 or 55%,â he said.The outcome was also closely tied to the performance of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), whose ability to clear the 5% threshold needed to enter the state parliament remained uncertain for several hours. Interim results eventually showed the party had crossed the threshold, meaning the AfD would not gain the additional seats it might otherwise have secured.The AfD was projected to win 39 of the 83 seats in Saxony-Anhaltâs state parliament, leaving it three seats short of the 42 required for an outright majority.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. https://panow.com/2026/10/11/109-migrant.text: This image provided by the International Organization for Migration shows authorities intervening after a migrant ship capsized near Guhere, north of Obock, in Djibouti, Saturday, Oct. 11, 2026. (Alexandre Coissac/IOM via AP) By The Canadian Press 139 migrants, including children, die after boat capsizes off Djibouti Oct 11, 2026 | 5:09 AM Share on Facebook Share on Bluesky Share on X Copy Link GENEVA (AP) — At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday. That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves but they won’t be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Alexandre Coissac, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti, told the AP via the phone. “What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation,” Coissac said. “They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened.” Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, “mainly because it was overcrowded.” “The local authorities did their best,” Coissac said, “but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore.” Elections Voting day approaches for RM residents 27m ago Raiders win 7-2, acquire Chmiel Raiders momentum starting to roll after statement win in Swift Current 9h ago Vigil tomorrow Prince Albert pays tribute to Pte Shaun Farrell with homecoming procession 14h ago He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support. “They’re all in a state of shock,” Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday, said. “I tried to talk to some of them but it’s very difficult.” Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive. At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations. The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said. The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise. Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait towards Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement. That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen , on the other side of the strait. “This is a devastating loss of life,” said Coissac. “This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities.” In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. That’s the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia. Over 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM’s Missing Migrants Project. “No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way,” IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. “We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down.” ___ Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: The newly released report was commissioned after the Brereton findings by former defence force chief – and SAS officer – Angus Campbell in 2021. Photograph: LS Paul Berry View image in fullscreen The newly released report was commissioned after the Brereton findings by former defence force chief – and SAS officer – Angus Campbell in 2021. Photograph: LS Paul Berry Australian military Australian SAS officers knew about unlawful ‘throwdowns’ on dead Afghans, report says Nothing done to stop planting weapons on dead Afghans, ADF inspector says, as ‘breakdown of command’ allowed ‘egregious behaviour’ Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Doherty Wed 28 Oct 2026 20.30 EDT First published on Wed 28 Oct 2026 18.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Some Australian SAS officers knew that soldiers under their command were using “throwdowns” – planting weapons on dead Afghan civilians to portray them as combatants – but did nothing to stop the unlawful practice, a previously unpublished military report has said. Posted online this week, the executive summary of a 2021 investigation into the “cultural context” of the special operations command by the inspector general of the Australian Defence Force (IGADF) is scathing about the “breakdown of command” and the erosion of military discipline during special forces operations in Afghanistan, which “resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour”. Defence had previously refused to release the report despite it being the subject of freedom of information requests and an attempt to force its disclosure in the Senate. A previously published IGADF report, the Brereton Inquiry, made public in 2020 , found credible information that Australian special forces personnel murdered 39 Afghan civilians and prisoners. But the Brereton report largely exonerated officers, saying the “criminal behaviour” it uncovered “was conceived, committed, continued, and concealed at patrol commander level”. Patrol commanders in the Australian SAS are not commissioned officers, they are typically corporals or sergeants. However, the newly released report, commissioned after the Brereton findings by former defence force chief – and SAS officer – Angus Campbell in 2021, found some SAS officers knew about alleged “unlawful behaviour” and did not act to stop them. “Officers with actual knowledge of misconduct in-theatre, including notably the use of throwdowns to effect in fraudulent reporting, or rumours of misconduct, did not take effective action to investigate and address these issues.” The unlawful behaviour identified by the IGADF revealed “a breakdown of command” and ineffective leadership. “The proper functioning of the ADF as a hierarchical system relies upon the enforcement of rules at all levels. A failure to do so has a corrosive effect on behaviours, morale and ultimately, military discipline, which in this case resulted in episodes of potential and actual egregious behaviour.” SAS officers allowed the regiment to develop an “uncontrolled ‘warrior’ ethos” and the long, grinding, nature of the Afghan conflict, to which a small cohort of SAS soldiers were repeatedly sent on dangerous, corrosive deployments, contributed to moral injury and impaired decision-making. “The group dynamic within a special forces deployment influences the shift in moral compass of some individuals,” the report said. “The incremental shift in moral compass in response to violence, killing, morally questionable decisions and unconventional features, can create moral injury.” The report found that the excessively secretive and insular nature of the SAS also contributed to worsening standards as did an “inversion” of the chain of command, where senior non-commissioned officers were able to dominate officers who were, ostensibly, their superiors. “This resulted in junior officers being effectively subservient to non-commissioned officers, and occupying a position which can best be described as ‘learned helplessness’.” The report cited the fact SAS soldiers were consistently allowed to drink alcohol while on deployment in Afghanistan – in defiance of orders imposed on others – “sent the strong signal to those involved that the rules did not apply to them”. The use of “throwdowns” was a known breach that officers failed to stop. “The unwillingness to challenge non-commissioned officers was particularly apparent from the breakdown of military discipline through a lack of proper supervision. The failure to address the widely known use of throwdowns is an example of this. “This was also a manifestation of a broader breakdown of military discipline within the SAS regiment. The tolerance of officers of overt non-compliance sent a powerful signal.” Similarly, soldiers wrote false reports of their actions on the battlefield, focused on rules of engagement and laced with circumlocution, which “assisted perpetrators of misconduct to conceal their actions”. “A particular manifestation was the use of variations of a standard phrase ‘manoeuvring to a position of tactical advantage’, to describe the actions of civilian ‘squirters’ as direct participants in hostilities, which justified engagement … under the rules of engagement. The expression was used with such regularity that it lost meaning.” The report’s executive summary says there was “a significant failure of good leadership and effective command” across the SAS commanders, and that the reporting systems designed to prevent misconduct had become “depleted and largely unreliable”, giving officers “a false level of assurance”. “The culture of the Special Operations Task Group … was not the cause of misconduct but created an environment which enabled misconduct by a few to occur.” The chief of the ADF Admiral Mark Hammond was interrogated on the report in senate estimates Thursday morning. He said he agreed with the report findings, stating there had been “serious failures” within the SAS and its command structure. He said the report revealed “unacceptable behaviour … it is extremely unprofessional, that behaviour is absolutely not in concert with our values, our professional standards, the behaviour that we expect of our personnel”. Hammond was asked specifically about the finding that legal officers within the defence force obstructed investigations into allegations of war crimes. “The behaviour you’re describing is completely unacceptable,” Hammond said. Greens Senator David Shoebridge argued there was a lack of accountability for the SAS leadership. “The thing that is eroding faith and trust… is this seeming accountability gap between what happens if you don’t have gold braid on your shoulders, where the book gets thrown at you … and the people who are in leadership positions who were either aware of it, or had the data that should have triggered that [awareness], and have not taken action.” Outside of parliament, opposition frontbencher and former SAS captain, Andrew Hastie, said the report’s findings resonated with his experience in the regiment. “I lived a lot of what I read in that report. There’s almost 50 findings, and a lot of it rings very true to me as a junior officer at the time.” Hastie told ABC radio officers were responsible for the actions of those they commanded. “In the end, if you hold a commission in the Australian Army, then you are accountable for those underneath you,” he said. “Maybe not directly for actions, but certainly there’s moral accountability, moral responsibility.” Explore more on these topics Australian military Afghanistan news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Don’t be stinky’: recruitment a ‘huge issue’ facing Aukus submarine program We want you!
